title: Security Reference Architecture for Cloud Data Mirrors
text:
Cloud Data Mirror RFC: your data, encrypted with your key, readable only by the AI you approve









Request for comments. Round 1 is open until 11 December 2026, 23:59 UTC.



What this is. A security reference architecture for cloud data mirrors: a private copy of a person’s messages and data that only the readers they choose, including their AI assistants, can search. AJS Consult LLC publishes it for open review.
How to take part

Read it. Start with the executive summary.
Comment or suggest changes. On any page: select text to comment on it, press Suggest edits to change the wording right on the page and send your changes, or comment at the end of the page. Suggestions and comments made with a GitHub account are credited to it.
Follow the review. Updates: sign up by email, use the feed, or watch on GitHub.
Found a security problem in the running service? Email aaron@matterboard.ai with SECURITY in the subject. Never post it in a comment.

title: 1. Executive summary
text:
Comment or suggest a change. Select any text to comment on it. Press Suggest edits to change the wording right on this page, then send your changes. Or comment at the end of the page with your GitHub account.
Suggest edits
How suggestions are credited · Edit the Markdown on GitHub

Today, AI assistants connect directly to a user’s private correspondence via a variety of partially and fully supported, secure (and insecure) connectors. Under this status quo, AI providers become the custodians of this data, to the end of enabling bleeding edge automation and research capabilities to their users. Simply put, users should not need to hand over custody of their data in exchange for access to the best AIs. This document proposes a security architecture for a messaging mirror that can be securely, safely and privately operated by the user themselves or by a trusted 3rd party.
The proposal. One random key is made on the user’s own computer, and messages are encrypted there before they are uploaded. Each device or AI the user approves gets its own token, and the server can open the data only while one of them is making a request, so a copy of the database alone is useless. This is not end-to-end encryption: the server sees what it serves while it serves it, and What it does not protect lists the limits.
The problem. Data ownership concerns are among the most significant impediments to the proliferation of beneficial AI, especially in security, safety and privacy critical use cases. There currently exists no complete security reference architecture to enable individuals or organizations to securely, safely and privately host their own data mirrors in a way that is integrated and compatible with AI assistants. Closed-source solutions to data mirroring require users to trust the implementation, and this document is meant to align users on “the right way” to achieve this goal so trust can be attained.
The alternative. Without a community effort to develop a security, privacy and safety standard around private data, the most likely outcome is for AIs to become more entrenched in their position as system of record for user’s private data optimally stored for use by AI. Private 3rd party companies hosting closed source messaging mirrors require the user to trust that bond, which is a non-starter for anyone hosting sensitive or mission critical data. As well, the technical requirements of building such data management systems require seasoned, credentialed software engineering veterans and are thus costly and/or out of reach for most potential users of powerful AI.
What is asked of you. Help us figure out what’s worth building that will actually get adopted because it is trusted. Attack the design. What it does not protect, the search leakage (question 1) and the questions for reviewers matter most.
Disclosure. The publisher, AJS Consult LLC, also builds a commercial product on this design; see Disclosures under Document control.

text:

The design has one goal: a copy of the stored data is useless without a credential the user approved. It does not hide data from the server while the server answers an approved request.



Who
Protected?




Someone who steals the database, a backup or a disk
Yes. They hold ciphertext, search tags and token hashes, and no key. The tags still leak some structure (see What it does not protect). Attachments are encrypted by the storage service under a key it does not keep, so a copy of the bucket is unreadable as well.


The operator’s staff reading stored data
Yes, in the same way


A reader or writer after the user revokes it
Yes, through the service: its token no longer finds a copy


A compromised server, or an operator who changes the server’s code
No. It sees the account key during any approved request and could keep it. Mitigated, not closed: the security-critical code is published, and the service is run to recognised cloud security standards (ISO/IEC 27017, the CSA Cloud Controls Matrix and NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5).


Malware on the user’s desktop
No. The desktop holds the account key.

The design exists to meet six requirements, and nothing in it serves anything else.








#
Requirement
How the design meets it




R1
The user controls the keys
The account key is made on the user’s desktop. A reader or writer gets access only when the user approves it, and loses it when the user revokes it.


R2
A collector node collects and pushes messages in real time, encrypted from the source
The node is the user’s desktop app (5.1.1) or a hosted bridge unlocked by the user’s key (5.1.2). The desktop encrypts each message under a content key derived from the account key, and computes its search tags, before it uploads. The bridge seals each message to the account’s public key, so it cannot read the mirror back. The database never receives plaintext from either. Attachments are the exception (see Decisions made to simplify).


R3
Data is secure at rest in the database
The database holds ciphertext, keyed tags and token hashes. Nothing in it opens without a token.


R4
Approved readers and writers can search, retrieve and update in near real time
Each holds a token that opens its own copy of the account key for one request. A message is searchable as soon as it is stored.


R5
Under 10 seconds from a user’s question to the AI’s first response
The mirror’s share is budgeted at 1 second at the 95th percentile. The rest belongs to the AI.


R6
Model outputs stay encrypted back to the user
Everything a model writes for the user is stored as a write under the content key, remembers its sources, and leaves the mirror in the clear only where the user chooses (5.3).

title: 4. The design on one page
text:

There is one key, one kind of token, and two algorithms: AES-256-GCM encrypts everything, and SHA-256 does the rest as a hash, as HMAC and as HKDF. Everything else follows from them.


Figure 4.1. The whole design: one account key, one kind of token, a database and a blob store · Text version 

One key. On installation, the desktop sync application asks the operating system for 256 random bits, and those bits are the “account key”. The user’s OS key store holds the account key and releases it only to approved application(s). The account key never encrypts anything itself. Instead, HKDF-SHA256 turns it into two working keys, one per job: (1) a content key that encrypts each message (AES-256-GCM) and (2) a tag key that computes the search tags (HMAC-SHA256). A third, the storage key, is derived the same way for attachments. They are re-derived whenever they are needed, so nothing extra is stored, and learning one working key reveals neither the other nor the account key. Because both come from the one account key, a reader that can open its copy of the account key can both read messages and search them.


Why this is current best practice: a full-strength random key from an approved generator (NIST SP 800-133 Rev. 2); one key per purpose, never one key for two jobs (NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev. 5, key separation); and working keys derived with HKDF (RFC 5869), the extract-then-expand construction NIST approves in SP 800-56C Rev. 2 and the one TLS 1.3 uses for all its keys (RFC 8446).


Encrypted at the source. The desktop app encrypts each message with AES-256-GCM, bound to the account and the message’s id, and computes its search tags with HMAC-SHA256. Only ciphertext and tags leave the desktop. A hosted bridge, where the user runs one, seals each message to the account’s public key instead and cannot read it back (5.1.2). Attachments are the exception: the desktop uploads them as they are, and the storage service encrypts each one under a storage key that is derived from the account key, supplied with the request and never kept (see Decisions made to simplify).


Why this is current best practice: AES-256-GCM is the NIST-approved authenticated encryption mode (SP 800-38D, over AES in FIPS 197), so tampering is detected, not just hidden. Binding each ciphertext to its account and message id as associated data follows the AEAD design in RFC 5116, which stops a stored ciphertext being swapped into another row or account. HMAC-SHA256 is the approved keyed hash (FIPS 198-1), and keyed tags over fragments are the classic construction for search over encrypted data (Song, Wagner and Perrig, IEEE S&P 2000). Its known limit, that equal fragments produce equal tags, is question 1, and GCM’s nonce limit is question 2.


One kind of token. Every reader or writer the user approves gets a random 256-bit token: a connected AI, the web app, a second device, a script. The server keeps the token’s SHA-256, to find it, and one copy of the account key locked under a key derived from the token (AES-256-GCM, the cipher that also encrypts messages). One token, one copy.


Why this is current best practice: high-entropy bearer tokens are the OAuth standard (RFC 6750), and short lifetimes with refresh-token rotation follow the OAuth security best current practice (RFC 9700). Keeping only a hash of each token means a database copy yields no usable credential, the same rule NIST SP 800-63B sets for stored passwords. Locking one copy of the account key per holder with AES-256-GCM, an authenticated cipher that NIST also approves for wrapping keys (NIST SP 800-38F) is envelope encryption, the pattern cloud key-management services use.


Search without plaintext. Inside an approved request the server unlocks the account key, turns the query into tags, finds candidates in an ordinary database index, and decrypts only those.


Why this is current best practice: keyed tags are the standard construction for search over encrypted data (Song, Wagner and Perrig, IEEE S&P 2000). Filtering on trigrams and then checking the real match is how production regex search works (Russ Cox, Regular Expression Matching with a Trigram Index). The known cost is access-pattern leakage (Cash et al., Leakage-Abuse Attacks Against Searchable Encryption, CCS 2015), which is why this design names it as a limit and asks reviewers about it (question 1).


Revocation is deletion. Deleting a token’s hash and its copy cuts that reader or writer off at once.


Why this is current best practice: revoking one holder deletes its only way to open the key through the service. Deleting every copy, as account deletion does, is cryptographic erase, a sanitization method NIST recognizes (SP 800-88 Rev. 1). Revoking a token server-side, effective on its next use, is what OAuth token revocation specifies (RFC 7009). Two gaps remain: backups hold old copies for up to 30 days, and the other copies of the same key stay valid (see What it does not protect).

The server never stores the account key, a token or plaintext. It holds the account key in memory only while it answers a request from an approved token. An attested worker, if the user unlocks one, is the exception: it holds its own key for the length of its lease (5.3).
One rule for every credential. Each credential has its own locked copy of the account key. Every hand-off opens the copy with the old credential, locks a new copy under the new one, and deletes the old. An OAuth authorization code, the web app’s connect code and a renewed token are all hand-offs of this kind, so the server never needs to store a token while one is in transit. A recovery code is the same thing on paper.

title: 5. How it works
text:
5.1 Key management lifecycle
The chain of joins. The service joins systems that were built separately, and each join decides who can read. End-to-end encryption survives a join only where the join point is one of the user’s own endpoints, and the whole chain is only as strong as its weakest hop.
Figure 5.1. The chain of joins: who can read at each join point, and what sets each hop’s guarantee · Text version
Why this is best practice. The IETF’s MIMI working group joins separately run messaging services by making every client a member of one end-to-end security state: servers relay ciphertext and take part only as senders who can authenticate, not read (draft-ietf-mimi-arch, over MLS, RFC 9420). A join point that decrypts and re-encrypts is a participant, and confidentiality is broken wherever content can be decrypted between the ends (draft-knodel-e2ee-definition, section 2). The security questions interoperability raises, identity, protocols and abuse, are laid out by Len, Ghosh, Grubbs and Rösler (2023). This design states the guarantee of every hop rather than claiming one for the whole chain.
The same machinery seen twice: first what happens to the account key, then what happens to the data.
The account key is created once on the desktop, opened only inside approved requests, changed only by adding or removing locked copies, and destroyed by deleting every copy.
Figure 5.2. Where the account key lives in the clear, and where only locked copies exist · Text version
Only a desktop keystore holds the account key at rest. The server holds it in memory for one request at a time; everything else holds a locked copy, a token, or nothing. An attested worker, if the user unlocks one, holds it in memory for the length of its lease (5.3).
Every change to who can read the mirror is a copy of the account key added or deleted; the account key itself changes only if it is rotated.
Every source is collected by a node that only the user’s key can unlock: the desktop app the user runs, or a bridge the service hosts for them. Both write into the same mirror, under the same account key. The two models differ in how the node is keyed, as set out below. The rest of this document says collector node for either.
Figure 5.3. Two ways to collect: the desktop node and the hosted bridge write into one mirror · Text version

title: 5. How it works
text:
5.1.1 The desktop node
The desktop node is the desktop app the user runs. It holds the account key, reads each source on the user’s machine, and encrypts and tags each message before upload. It is the strongest pattern: an end-to-end encrypted chat stays end-to-end encrypted as far as the user’s own device. Its cost is that every user must run one, and the mirror is only as fresh as that machine. The account key’s life on it has five operations.

5.1.1.1 Create
On first run, the desktop app generates the account key from 256 random bits and stores it in the OS keystore. Where the platform offers it, the keystore releases the key only after the user proves presence, with a biometric or the device passcode, when the app starts. The app asks for the same proof before each approval of a new reader or writer. It then signs in, receives its own desktop token, wraps the account key under a key derived from that token, and uploads only that locked copy. The server stores the copy beside the token’s hash; it never sees the account key and never keeps the token.


Figure 5.4. Create: the desktop makes the account key and uploads only a locked copy · Text version 
Why this is best practice. The key is made from a cryptographically secure random source on the device that will hold it, which is what NIST SP 800-133 Rev. 2 recommends, and it is stored in the OS key store, hardware-backed where the platform offers it, rather than in a file. The server receives only a wrapped copy (NIST SP 800-38F), so nothing the server stores can open the data. That separation is the core idea of client-side and envelope encryption.


5.1.1.2 Read
A reader’s request carries its token. The server finds the reader’s locked copy by the token’s hash, derives the unwrapping key from the token with HKDF, and opens the account key in memory. It looks up the query’s tags, decrypts only the candidate rows and returns the results. When the request ends, the account key is dropped; nothing of it is written to disk or logs.


Figure 5.5. Read: a token opens its copy of the account key for one request · Text version 
Why this is best practice. The key is opened only in memory, only for one request, and then dropped. That follows NIST SP 800-57 Part 1: keep plaintext keys out of persistent storage and out of logs, and limit how long they exist. The unwrapping key is derived from the token with HKDF (RFC 5869), the standard way to turn a high-entropy secret into a key, and the server looks tokens up by hash, so its stored data holds no usable credential.


5.1.1.3 Update
When the user approves a new reader or writer, the approval happens inside a session that already holds the account key. The server makes a new token, wraps the account key under a key derived from it, stores that copy beside the new token’s hash, and hands the new token to the new holder once. Renewing a token follows the same steps, then deletes the old token’s hash and copy. The account key itself does not change.


Figure 5.6. Update: a new reader or writer gets its own token and its own locked copy · Text version 
Why this is best practice. Granting access means wrapping the same key once more, not re-encrypting data or sharing one credential among holders. This is envelope encryption, the pattern cloud key-management services use, and it means every holder can be revoked on its own. Handing a new token over once and rotating it on renewal follows the OAuth security best current practice (RFC 9700).


5.1.1.4 Expire
Every token has an end time, stored beside its hash. The server refuses an expired token on every request, and a periodic sweep then deletes the expired token’s hash and its copy of the account key. A holder renews before its end time by presenting its current token, which follows Update; a refresh token presented twice revokes its whole chain. The lifetime for each kind of holder is question 4. Backups can still hold an expired copy for up to 30 days (see What it does not protect).


Figure 5.7. Expire: an expired token is refused and its copy is deleted · Text version 
Why this is best practice. Every token has a fixed lifetime, and its copy of the key is deleted when that lifetime ends, so a leaked token stops working without anyone acting. Bounded lifetimes are what RFC 9700 recommends for tokens, and NIST calls them cryptoperiods (SP 800-57 Part 1).


5.1.1.5 Delete
The user ends access in one of three ways, each from an approved device:

Revoke one reader or writer (an AI, a browser session, a script). The server deletes that token’s hash and its copy of the account key. That holder is cut off at once, and every other holder keeps working.
Remove a lost device. The same deletion, for the device’s token. Recovery then runs as an Update from a device the user still has.
Delete the account. The server deletes every copy and every row. With no copy of the account key left, nothing live can open the mirror.

Backups still hold old copies until they expire, up to 30 days. If every holder is lost, the next desktop makes a new account key and collects again from the sources.


Figure 5.8. Delete: access ends when a token’s hash and its copy are deleted · Text version 
Why this is best practice. Deleting every copy of the key, as account deletion does, is cryptographic erase, a sanitization method NIST recognizes (SP 800-88 Rev. 1). It works at once, even when ciphertext remains in storage the user cannot reach. Revoking a single holder is weaker: it ends that holder’s access through the service, but other copies of the same key remain. Revocation takes effect server-side on the token’s next use, as OAuth token revocation specifies (RFC 7009). The known exception is backups, which keep old copies for up to 30 days.



5.1.2 The hosted bridge
A hosted bridge does the desktop’s collecting on the service’s machines, so the user needs no desktop running. For an end-to-end encrypted chat it is a server-side bridge: a linked device of the user’s account that sees every message it carries. The design cannot change that. What it can do is make sure the bridge runs only for the user, unlocked by the user’s key.
The same five operations apply to the bridge. Each is described below only where it differs from the desktop node (5.1.1). One difference sits behind all of them: the bridge never holds the account key. It holds a bridge key, which opens only the bridge’s own state, and it holds that key on a lease.

5.1.2.1 Create
The bridge makes no account key, and no locked copy of the account key is made for it. The account key already exists (5.1.1.1). What is made for the bridge is a bridge key, derived from the account key with HKDF. At rest, the bridge’s state (its linked-device keys, session state and source credentials) is ciphertext under that key, so the bridge starts locked: a copy of that state cannot run, and cannot fork a chat’s message ratchet. For writing, the bridge is given only the account’s public key (5.2.1).


5.1.2.2 Read
A reader’s token opens the account key in the server’s memory for one request (5.1.1.2). No request opens the account key for the bridge. What is opened is the bridge key, and the user’s device opens it only after checking what the bridge runs. The bridge runs in a confidential virtual machine. On start it makes a one-time key pair and an attestation that binds the public key to the measurement of its image. An approved device of the user checks that measurement against a published, append-only log of release images, then seals the bridge key to the one-time public key. The bridge then holds the bridge key in memory for the length of its lease, not for one request. After any restart it stays locked until a device unlocks it again, and the chat services hold messages meanwhile.
The bridge key opens nothing in the mirror. The bridge holds neither the content key nor the tag key, so it cannot read back what it writes (5.2.1).


Figure 5.9. Unlocking the hosted bridge: the user’s device checks the image, then seals the bridge key under a lease · Text version 


5.1.2.3 Update
Approving a new reader or writer is unchanged (5.1.1.3). It happens inside a session that holds the account key, so the bridge can approve no one. What is renewed for the bridge is its unlock rather than a token: the user’s approved devices renew the lease in the background.


5.1.2.4 Expire
A token expires at the server, which refuses it and then deletes its copy of the account key (5.1.1.4). The bridge’s unlock expires at the bridge. The lease ends after a set time (proposed: 7 days), and when no device has renewed it, the bridge erases the bridge key and stops. It is then locked again, as it was at Create.


5.1.2.5 Delete
Deleting a token’s hash and its copy of the account key is enough to cut off a reader (5.1.1.5). It is not enough for the bridge, because the bridge is also a device on the user’s chat accounts. Revoking the bridge ends its lease, unlinks its device from each chat service, and rotates the bridge key. Without the unlink, the bridge’s identity at the chat service outlives anything the service controls. Deleting the account revokes the bridge in the same way.



5.1.3 Which sources each pattern carries








Source
Desktop node
Hosted bridge




Hosted mail, calendars, contacts, and device or industrial clouds
Yes
Yes. These sources were never end-to-end encrypted, so the bridge adds the service as one more party that sees them, not a new kind of exposure


End-to-end encrypted chats whose service allows a third-party linked client
Yes
Yes, as a linked device (5.1.2), within that service’s terms


End-to-end encrypted chats that require the vendor’s own hardware or client
Yes
No



Why this is best practice. Releasing a secret only to a machine that proves which code it runs is remote attestation (RFC 9334, the RATS architecture). Cloud key services already release keys only to an attested image (Google Confidential Space), and having the user’s device check the image against a public log before it sends anything is how Apple Private Cloud Compute works. Sealing to a public key with HPKE (RFC 9180) lets a writer add data it can never read back. None of this makes the bridge an endpoint by the definition in Knodel et al. (2025); that is question 8.

title: 5. How it works
section: 5.2 How data moves
text:
5.2 How data moves
Five flows cover everything the system does. In each one, the account key is opened only inside a request that presents an approved token.

5.2.1 Collect and push
New messages are locked on the collector node before they go anywhere, so the service stores only ciphertext, which opens only inside an approved request.

The collector node reads a new message from a source: mail, messaging apps, team chat, a calendar.
It encrypts the message with the keys its model holds (5.1), so that only an approved request can open it.
It uploads the result over TLS. The server stores it and cannot open it without an approved token.
The message is searchable as soon as it is stored and tagged.



Figure 5.10. Collect and push: messages are encrypted on the collector node before upload · Text version 
Only ciphertext and tags leave the collector node; the server cannot open them without an approved token.
A desktop node encrypts and tags. It holds the account key, so it encrypts each message under the content key and computes its search tags before upload. The message is searchable as soon as it is stored.
A hosted bridge can write but not read back. It seals each message with HPKE to the account’s public key, an X25519 key pair whose private half is derived from the account key. Only an approved request can open it; that request re-encrypts the message under the content key and computes its tags, so the mirror keeps one format at rest. A compromised bridge exposes the messages passing through it while it is compromised, not the mirror’s history. The bridge holds no tag key (question 9).


Figure 5.11. Writing through the hosted bridge: each message is sealed to the account’s public key · Text version 
Why this is best practice. Encrypting on the client before upload, so the storage provider holds only ciphertext, is the model behind end-to-end encrypted storage and client-side encryption. Each message is sealed with AES-256-GCM (NIST SP 800-38D), an authenticated cipher that detects any change to the ciphertext, and it is bound to its account and message ids as associated data (RFC 5116), so a row cannot be moved to another account or message. TLS protects the upload in transit (RFC 8446).


5.2.2 Approve a reader or writer
Nothing gets access unless the user says yes, and every approved AI, browser or device gets its own key that can be cancelled on its own.

The user approves it: OAuth consent for an AI, the web app opened from the desktop, or a matching code for a second device.
Inside the user’s own approved session, the server makes a new token and a copy of the account key locked under it.
The token is handed to the new reader or writer once. The server keeps only its hash.



Figure 5.12. Approve a reader or writer: one approval, one token, one locked copy · Text version 
The server keeps only the token’s hash; the token itself is handed over once.
Why this is best practice. AI clients are approved through OAuth consent with PKCE, as the OAuth security best current practice requires (RFC 9700), and a second device is approved by comparing a short code on both screens, a relative of the device flow in RFC 8628, with the cross-device risks that RFC 10027 sets out. Giving each holder its own token and its own wrapped copy of the key is least privilege: no credential is shared, so each one can be revoked alone. Storing only a hash of each token means a database copy yields no usable credential, as NIST SP 800-63B requires for stored passwords.


5.2.3 Search and retrieve
An approved AI gets answers in well under a second, and the data is unlocked only for that one question, then locked again.

A reader sends a query with its token.
The server finds the token’s copy by its hash and unlocks the account key for this request.
It turns the query into tags, finds the candidates in the index, decrypts only those, and checks the real match.
It returns the results and drops the account key.



Figure 5.13. Search and retrieve: the account key is opened for one request only · Text version 
Only the candidate rows are decrypted, and the account key lives only for the request.
Why this is best practice. Search runs on keyed tags, the standard construction for searching encrypted data (Song, Wagner and Perrig, IEEE S&P 2000). The query is reduced to trigrams and the real match is checked afterwards, as in production regex search (Russ Cox, trigram index). Holding the key in memory for one request only follows NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 on limiting how long plaintext keys exist. The known cost is access-pattern leakage (Cash et al., CCS 2015), which question 1 puts to reviewers.


5.2.4 Update
Edits by an approved AI or by the user are locked the moment they are saved, and every other reader sees them on its next request.

A writer sends a change with its token: an AI’s tool call, or an edit on the web app.
The server unlocks the account key, encrypts the change, recomputes its tags and stores it.
Every reader sees it on its next request.



Figure 5.14. Update: a writer’s change is encrypted on the server inside its request · Text version 
Writes follow the same rule as reads: the account key is opened only inside the writer’s request.
Why this is best practice. A write uses the same authenticated encryption as a read, so the server never stores an edited row in the clear. Every write gets a fresh random nonce, which is what keeps AES-GCM secure when the same key encrypts many messages (NIST SP 800-38D, section 8). The tags are recomputed with HMAC-SHA256 (FIPS 198-1), so the search index never falls out of step with the content.


5.2.5 Revoke and recover
Cutting off an AI or a lost device takes effect at once and touches no one else; a replacement device is approved like any other.

Revoke. Deleting a token’s hash and copy cuts that reader or writer off at once.
A lost desktop. From another approved device the user revokes it, then approves a new desktop, which receives the account key through its own copy.
The only desktop lost. A recovery code made at setup is one more token, printed and kept offline, with its own locked copy. Presented from a new desktop, it approves that desktop. Without one, the mirror starts again with a new account key even if AI readers still hold tokens, because a reader’s token cannot approve a device.
Every holder lost. The mirror cannot be read. A new desktop makes a new account key and collects again from the sources.



Figure 5.15. Revoke and recover: one deletion cuts a holder off, and recovery needs another approved device · Text version 
Cutting off a reader is one deletion; a replacement desktop is approved like any other holder.
Why this is best practice. Revoking a token server-side, so that it fails on its next use, is what OAuth token revocation specifies (RFC 7009). Deleting that token’s copy ends its access through the service. Only deleting every copy is cryptographic erase, the sanitization method NIST recognizes (SP 800-88 Rev. 1). Recovering through another approved device, rather than through a reset the operator controls, keeps the operator unable to open the data. End-to-end encrypted services use the same approach, and when every holder is lost the honest result is that the data cannot be read.

title: 5. How it works
section: 5.3 Model outputs stay encrypted back to the user
text:
5.3 Model outputs stay encrypted back to the user
Everything a model writes for the user is stored and delivered under the same rule as the user’s own messages: readable only through a credential the user approved.

Every output is a write. A briefing, a summary, a note a model keeps between runs, a title or a label is encrypted under the content key, with its own tags, inside the request or worker that made it (5.2.4). Nothing a model writes is stored in the clear, including fields that look like metadata, such as a briefing’s title.
Outputs remember their sources. Each derived row records, encrypted, the ids of the rows it was made from. Deleting or revoking a source deletes, or marks for regeneration, what was derived from it, so a summary cannot outlive the messages it summarizes.
Unattended output runs only where the user’s key is unlocked. In order of preference: when the user opens it, inside that session; inside the collector node’s own push; or in an attested worker unlocked and leased exactly like the hosted bridge (5.1.2), with its own key and lease so it can be revoked on its own. Unlike the bridge, the worker reads the mirror, so it is the one place unattended reading happens.
Delivery carries a pointer by default. A notification says a briefing is ready and links to it; the text opens inside an approved session. Sending the full text to a channel that can read it, such as email or a chat bot, is a choice the user makes for each delivery, labelled as plaintext to that channel. Sending it to other people is the user’s own disclosure.
Outputs are rendered as untrusted. Incoming messages from anyone shape what a model writes, so an output may carry an injected instruction or link. Outputs are shown without remote content, and links are shown in full or limited to an allowlist, so an output cannot send data out just by being displayed.



Figure 5.16. Model outputs: stored as encrypted writes, delivered as a pointer unless the user chooses full text · Text version 
Why this is best practice. A summary is a function of the content, and Knodel et al. (2025) treat any non-trivial function of protected content as that content, so it needs the same protection. Prompt injection through content a model reads is the first risk in the OWASP Top 10 for LLM applications, and it becomes exploitable when private data, untrusted content and a way to send data out meet in one system (Willison, “The lethal trifecta”). A pointer by default and rendering without remote content remove the third.

This is encryption controlled by the user’s keys, not end-to-end encryption: the server decrypts inside each approved request. By the definition in Knodel et al. (2025), a cloud machine is never an endpoint however it is keyed, so neither a hosted bridge (5.1.2) nor an attested worker (5.3) makes it end-to-end encryption (question 8). The limits follow.







Limit
Consequence




The server holds the account key and the results while it answers
A compromised server can capture the account key from any approved request. That one key opens the whole mirror, past and future, until the key is rotated. Proving which code the server runs (attestation) would close this; it is not in this design. Mitigation: the security-critical code (whatever handles keys, tokens or plaintext) is published, so anyone can check what the server is meant to do, and the service is run to the cloud security standards named in What it defends against, whose controls include least privilege, separation of duties, and reviewed, logged changes to production code. These make a compromise or a rogue change harder to carry out and easier to detect. They do not prove what the running server does.


AI providers see what they retrieve and what they write
Their handling of prompts and outputs, including retention, is outside this design


Search tags reveal which messages share a fragment
The tags are deterministic and overlap, so a thief of the database may recover text from fragment frequencies alone, and more with some known plaintext (question 1). Sizes and times are visible too.


A stolen token works until it is revoked
Expiry limits the damage (question 4)


Malware on the desktop sees everything
The desktop holds the account key


Backups keep deleted copies until they expire
A revoked token can still open its copy in a backup taken earlier, for up to 30 days


Revoking one holder is access control, not erasure
Other copies of the same key remain, and a holder that paired its token with a copy of the database keeps the key. Only deleting every copy, or rotating the key, erases.


Every token opens the whole account key
What a holder may do (read only, one source, approve others) is enforced by the server’s rules, not by cryptography


Tokens, queries and results are plaintext in the server’s memory
They must be kept out of logs, traces and error reports. Whatever ends TLS in front of the server sees tokens too. Mitigation: the implementation’s source code is published, and automated tests plant marker values in tokens, queries and results and fail if a marker reaches a log, a trace, an error report or stored data. Publishing the source shows what the code does; proving that the running server is that code is what attestation would add (question 7).


The mirror is only as fresh as its collector node
While the collector node is off or locked, nothing new is collected


Search needs a fixed fragment of three or more characters
A query without one cannot use the index. It must be refused, or answered by decrypting every row.


Attachments are encrypted by the storage service, not on the desktop
The storage service sees each file in the clear while it handles an upload or a read. At rest, a file opens only with the storage key, which is derived from the account key inside an approved request. The bucket’s access policy stays as a second line.


A hosted bridge sees what it carries
While unlocked, the bridge sees every message passing through it, and so does anyone who controls its machine if attestation fails. It cannot start without the user’s device, and cannot read the mirror’s history (5.1.2).


A hosted bridge is a device on the user’s chat accounts
The other people in a conversation agreed to the user’s devices, not to a hosted one, and are not told. Its identity at the chat service lasts until it is unlinked, and a chat service’s terms may forbid it.


Attestation trusts the hardware maker
The hosted bridge and the attested worker are only as sound as the confidential-computing hardware and its maker’s keys.


Outputs are shaped by untrusted inputs
An injected instruction in an incoming message can steer what a model writes. The rendering rules limit what an output can send out (5.3); they do not stop the model being misled.


Outputs sent to a channel are plaintext to that channel
A mail or chat service sees any output the user chooses to send it in full.

These choices keep the design small. Each has a cost, stated here so reviewers can challenge it.








Decision
What it removes
What it costs

Server-side collectors that run without the user’s key
The hosted bridge brings back public-key sealing (HPKE) for writes it cannot read back, and it means something only with attestation and a lease (5.1.2)


The token is its own secret
Separate unlock secrets. SHA-256 of the token finds its copy; a key derived from the token with HKDF opens it, and knowing one gives nothing about the other.
A leaked token both identifies and unlocks, exactly as a leaked token-and-secret pair did before


Support is just another reader
The operator’s hardware-held support key. To get help, the user approves a support reader with an end time, like any other.
Its use is recorded in the service’s own log rather than by the cloud provider’s audit log


Background AI work needs a reader or an attested worker
Server-side processing the user never unlocked. Triage, filing and briefings run on the desktop, inside a reader’s request, or in a worker the user unlocked under a lease (5.3).
While no reader is active and no lease is live, nothing is processed


Attachments are encrypted by the storage service, under a key derived from the account key
Encrypting and chunking every file on the desktop
The storage service sees each file in the clear while it handles a request, and it must accept a key supplied per request. The bucket cannot hand out direct links, because every read needs the key.

title: 9. Questions for reviewers
text:

These nine are where review is wanted most.

Search leakage. Is a keyed trigram index acceptable for this threat model, or should tag sets be padded?
Nonce budget. One content key encrypts every message for the account’s life with random 96-bit nonces, and NIST SP 800-38D limits that to 2³² uses per key. The largest account today holds about 1.6 million messages, far below that. Proposed answer: derive a new content key each year with HKDF from the account key and the year, so the limit applies per year and nothing extra is stored. Is that enough, or is a cipher that tolerates nonce reuse (AES-GCM-SIV, XAES-256-GCM) still worth adding?
Rotating the account key. Proposed answer: rotation is a re-push. The desktop makes a new account key, re-encrypts the mirror under it, including what writers added, uploads it again and deletes the old copies. That is the same path as when every holder is lost. It costs a full upload, so it is for a suspected compromise, not a schedule. Is that acceptable, or are data keys wrapped by the account key worth their extra machinery?
Token lifetimes. What expiry and renewal should each kind have: desktop, AI access and refresh, web app session, script?
A second desktop. Is a matching code shown on both screens enough to approve one, given the cross-device risks set out in RFC 10027? And how should the new desktop’s token reach it without the server storing it: handed to a waiting request in memory, or sealed to a key the new desktop sends?
Support audit. Is the service’s own log enough for support access, or is an independent audit worth a second key?
Attestation. Is proving which code the server runs worth adding later, to close the first limit? For the hosted bridge and the attested worker it is not optional: is the unlock in 5.1.2, where the user’s device checks the image against a published log before it seals the bridge key, the right shape?
What a hosted endpoint is. By the definition in Knodel et al. (2025), a cloud machine is never endpoint-local, however it is keyed, so this design is not end-to-end encryption, and a hosted bridge does not make it so. The MIMI architecture treats a member as any client that holds the group’s keys. Is a hosted endpoint, keyed by the user, attested and on a lease, an endpoint of the user’s end-to-end encrypted systems, or a third party? Views from the MIMI working group and CFRG are especially welcome.
Searching what the bridge writes. The hosted bridge holds no tag key, so its messages become searchable only when the next approved request, or the desktop, tags them. Is that delay acceptable, or should the bridge hold the tag key, trading the leak in question 1 for search at once?

Figure 4.1. The whole design: one account key, one kind of token, a database and a blob store
Every diagram in this document, written out: a description in words, for screen readers and search, and its source in Mermaid, which GitHub draws and anyone can edit in a pull request. The pictures in the chapters are exported from the editor’s document; these text versions are kept in step with them, and the sync tool reports any picture that has changed since its text version was last checked.
Plaintext exists only on the collector node and inside an approved request
In 4. The design on one page. One account key. The collector encrypts or seals messages before upload, and each reader or writer opens its own copy. The collector node reads the sources (mail, chats, calendars). It is either the desktop app, which keeps the key, encrypts each message and computes search tags, or a hosted bridge, which seals what it cannot read back. It sends ciphertext and tags, and attachments as they are, to the server. Readers and writers (AI assistants, the web app, second devices and scripts), each with its own token, send a token and request to the server. The server finds the token’s copy, opens the key per request, searches and decrypts hits, returns the results and drops the key afterwards. It stores and looks up ciphertext, search tags, token hashes and locked copies of the key in the database, and stores and reads attachments in the blob store, encrypted under the storage key, which is sent with each request and never kept. The server never stores the account key, a token or plaintext. The blob store sees each attachment in the clear while it handles a request, and keeps only ciphertext.

text:
Figure 5.1. The chain of joins: who can read at each join point, and what sets each hop’s guarantee
Each join decides who can read; end-to-end encryption ends at the mirror
In 5. How it works. The chain of joins. Sources (end-to-end encrypted chats, hosted mail, calendars, contacts and device clouds) feed the collector node. On that hop the guarantee is set by the chat’s own protocol, or by the source’s provider. At the collector node, with the desktop node only the user’s devices can read, and with a hosted bridge the bridge can read as well. The collector feeds the mirror. On that hop the guarantee is set by this design, encryption under the user’s keys. At the mirror the server reads, inside an approved request only. End-to-end encryption ends here. From the mirror, data goes to an AI reader, where the AI provider reads and its terms and retention apply, and to a delivery channel, where the user sends an output, and that service and any recipient can read.

text:
Figure 5.2. Where the account key lives in the clear, and where only locked copies exist
The account key exists in the clear in only three places
In 5. How it works. Where the account key lives, where only a locked copy lives, and where it never goes. In the clear, the key exists only in the desktop OS keystore, at rest on each approved desktop and made on the first one, in server memory, with its derived keys, for one approved request only, and in an attested worker, in memory for the length of its lease, if the user unlocks one. Only a locked copy is in the database, one copy per approved token wrapped under a key from it, and in backups, where deleted copies stay until the backup expires, up to 30 days. The AIs, web app and scripts hold a token but never the key, and the server unlocks it for them. AI providers see only the results they asked for. A hosted bridge holds a bridge key derived from the account key, for its lease, never the key itself. Logs and operator staff hold no key, no token and no plaintext. A token opens only its own copy, so deleting that copy cuts its holder off at once. With a hosted bridge the key still rests only on the user’s desktop, and the bridge holds a derived key.

section: Figure 5.3. Two ways to collect: the desktop node and the hosted bridge write into one mirror
text:
Figure 5.3. Two ways to collect: the desktop node and the hosted bridge write into one mirror
Two collectors, one mirror: the bridge can write but not read back
In 5. How it works. Two ways to collect. Both are unlocked only by the user’s key and write into the same mirror. The sources (hosted mail, calendars, contacts, device clouds and encrypted chats) feed either the desktop node or the hosted bridge. The desktop node runs on the user’s own machine, holds the account key, and encrypts and tags before upload. The hosted bridge runs on the service’s machines, is locked until the user’s device unlocks it on a lease, and seals messages it cannot read back. Both write to the mirror: the same mirror for both, under one account key, with one format at rest. An approved request opens each sealed message, re-encrypts it under the content key and computes its tags. Encrypted chats that need the vendor’s own hardware or client are carried by the desktop node only.

section: Figure 5.9. Unlocking the hosted bridge: the user’s device checks the image, then seals the bridge key under a lease
text:
Figure 5.9. Unlocking the hosted bridge: the user’s device checks the image, then seals the bridge key under a lease
The bridge stays locked until the user’s device has checked what it runs
In 5. How it works. Unlocking the hosted bridge. The hosted bridge starts locked: its state is ciphertext under the bridge key. On start it makes a one-time key pair and an attestation of its image. It sends the approved device an attestation binding the one-time public key to the image’s measurement. The approved device checks the measurement against the published, append-only log of release images. It then sends the bridge the bridge key, sealed to the one-time public key. The unlock is a lease (proposed: 7 days). Approved devices renew it in the background. If none does, the bridge erases the bridge key and stops. After any restart the bridge is locked again until a device unlocks it.

Figure 5.11. Writing through the hosted bridge: each message is sealed to the account’s public key
The bridge seals each message to the account’s public key and cannot read it back

text:
Figure 5.16. Model outputs: stored as encrypted writes, delivered as a pointer unless the user chooses full text
Model outputs are stored encrypted; full text leaves only by the user’s choice
In 5. How it works. Model outputs: where they are made, how they are stored and how they are delivered. Output is made in one of three places, in order of preference: in the user’s open session, in the collector node’s own push, or in an attested worker on a lease. It is stored as a write, encrypted under the content key with its own tags. It records its source rows, encrypted, and its titles and labels are included. It is delivered as a pointer by default: a notification links to it, and the text opens inside an approved session. Full text goes to a channel only where the user chooses, for each delivery, as labelled plaintext to that channel. Outputs are shown without remote content, and links are shown in full or limited to an allowlist. Deleting or revoking a source deletes, or marks for regeneration, what was derived from it.

Figure 6.1. Latency budget: targets at the 95th percentile, not measurements
Encryption adds well under a second, and the answer lands inside the 10-second budget
In 6. Latency budget. Question to first response is 7.4 seconds at the 95th percentile, of which the mirror is 0.405 seconds. These are targets, not measurements. The AI provider reads the question and calls the mirror in an assumed 3 seconds. The mirror then takes 0.405 seconds of its 1-second budget: 0.2 seconds for the request to the server and back over the network, 0.005 seconds on the server to find the token and unlock the key, 0.1 seconds in the database to look up the query’s tags, and 0.1 seconds on the server to decrypt and check 200 candidates. The AI provider then writes the first words from the results in an assumed 4 seconds, so the first response arrives at 7.4 seconds, inside the 10-second budget.

In Appendix A. Single or multi-tenant. Each user’s key stays on their desktop in both designs, and colours mark whose key locks which rows. With one shared database, users A, B and C, holding keys A, B and C, all use one shared server, which opens key A, B or C inside each user’s request, and one shared database with row-level security, where user A’s rows are locked under key A, user B’s under key B and user C’s under key C. A server breach sees every active user’s requests. There is one system to run, and metadata is visible to the operator. With one instance per user, user A uses server A, which holds key A only, and database A, which holds user A’s rows under key A, and the same for users B and C. A server breach sees one user’s requests. There is one system per user to run and pay for.
